_about: Curated explanations shown next to library results by analysis/library_report.py. status: 'verified' = backed by the evidence given; 'hypothesis' = plausible but not yet confirmed (say how to confirm). device is a glob on device_id; workload/library may be '*'. Add a note only with evidence.

notes.note: torch's fp32 linear layers (MKL GEMV) stream only ~25-35 GB/s at batch-1 decode on AMD EPYC, i.e. about one core's worth of bandwidth; OpenBLAS sgemv on the same tensors streams 218-285 GB/s. That the slowdown is inside MKL's AMD code path is a hypothesis (MKL_VERBOSE would show the dispatched kernel).
notes.plain: On AMD processors, PyTorch's default math library (Intel MKL) reads the model weights at roughly one core's speed when generating a single token; OpenBLAS uses the full memory speed.
notes.evidence: c6525-100g campaign c_amd_c6525_100g_20261111T0036Z, llama3-8b fp32 batch-1 decode: torch/MKL 0.74 tok/s (23 GB/s), OpenBLAS 3.21 (98 GB/s, 78% of 125), BLIS 0.85 (26 GB/s). Intel c6620, same problem: torch/MKL 6.58 tok/s (201 GB/s), so MKL's GEMV is fast on Intel. r6615 campaign c_amd_r6615_20261111T0632Z, same problem: torch/MKL 0.9 vs OpenBLAS 9.1 tok/s (BLIS 1.2).

notes.note: Batch-8 decode was 9-13% of bandwidth with all three libraries in the first r6615 test (before commit 72ab4db). The cause was the harness's attention step, not the BLAS: decode attention is now batched matmuls over an in-place KV cache. After the fix, BLIS's small-GEMM path is the fastest at batch 8 on all three CPUs.
notes.plain: When several tokens are generated at once, BLIS handles the small matrix shapes best on all three processors.
notes.evidence: llama3-8b fp32 batch-8 decode, campaigns of 2026-11-11: c6525-100g BLIS 18.9 tok/s (81 GB/s, 65% of 125) vs OpenBLAS 10.4, torch 5.8; c6620 BLIS 32.9 (141 GB/s, 66% of 214) vs OpenBLAS 19.2, torch 18.3. r6615 campaign: BLIS 43.0 tok/s vs OpenBLAS 21.1, torch 14.0 (the test session before the fix measured 10.8 tok/s with BLIS).

notes.note: Ubuntu 22.04's BLIS 0.8.1 has no Zen 4 kernels: it reported arch=generic and ran sgemm at ~960 GFLOP/s. scripts/setup_node.sh now builds upstream BLIS 2.1 (Zen 3 kernels) only on such CPUs; with it BLIS is the fastest fp64 GEMM library on Zen 4.
notes.evidence: r6615 2026-11-11: distro BLIS 0.8.1 arch=generic 960 vs BLIS 2.1 arch=zen3 2923 GFLOP/s (sgemm 4096 probe). Campaign c_amd_r6615_20261111T0632Z fp64: BLIS wins 4/4 sizes (n=4096: 1616 vs torch/MKL 1524, OpenBLAS 1308); rows record 'BLIS 2.1 arch=zen3'.
notes.plain: On AMD Zen 4, BLIS (built from its newest release) is the fastest library for 64-bit matrix multiply at every size.

notes.note: On Zen 4 fp32 GEMM the three libraries are within ~10% of each other and the winner changes with size (PyTorch/MKL at n=1024-2048, BLIS at 4096, OpenBLAS at 8192); BLIS wins fp64. The first r6615 test (BLIS 0.8.1) had OpenBLAS fp32 / MKL fp64.
notes.evidence: Campaign c_amd_r6615_20261111T0632Z fp32 GFLOP/s: n=1024 torch 2582 / BLIS 2391 / OpenBLAS 2304; n=8192 OpenBLAS 3469 / BLIS 3353 / torch 3209.

notes.note: The native direct convolution (filter size a compile-time constant, all K*K taps unrolled, vectorised x loop) wins every size: neural-network convolution libraries are not built for one small filter over a large image.
notes.plain: Our own kernel wins: neural-network libraries are built for many small images and filters, not for one small filter over a large image.
notes.evidence: r6615 campaign c_amd_r6615_20261111T0632Z: native wins 18/18 problems at 14-42% of the theoretical fp32 peak; next best OpenCV at 0.04-0.79x of native. V100 c_v100_20261110: native wins 18/18 vs cuDNN (median 0.42x).

notes.note: torch CPU conv2d for this shape (groups = channels, one 3/5/7 filter) IS oneDNN (verified: jit_dw depthwise kernel, ONEDNN_VERBOSE on Xeon Gold 5512U), but each call also reorders the whole image into oneDNN's blocked layout and back. That extra memory traffic is the likely reason it stays near ~160 Mpx/s (AMD) regardless of filter size: hypothesis; confirm by timing the reorders (ONEDNN_VERBOSE exec times).
notes.evidence: r6615 campaign c_amd_r6615_20261111T0632Z: 154-168 Mpx/s for every k at c=1, 67-83 at c=3, across 1024^2..8192^2 (the same as the earlier test session).

notes.note: Rows collected before commit d51fa7e ran OpenCV on ONE core (torch's OpenMP binding pins the main thread, and OpenCV's pthread pool inherited it). Only compare OpenCV rows from d51fa7e or later.
notes.evidence: r6615: filter2D 8192^2 k=5 634 Mpx/s pinned vs 6109 standalone; after the fix the sweep measured 12004 Mpx/s.

notes.note: OpenCV's bilateralFilter beats our native kernel on every CPU size once it runs on all cores (fixed in d51fa7e; rows before that ran on one core). The earlier claim 'native 7x faster than OpenCV' was an artefact of that bug.
notes.plain: OpenCV's filter beats our own kernel at almost every size once it uses all processor cores.
notes.evidence: Campaigns of 2026-11-11: native kernel at 0.19x (c6620) and 0.22x (c6525-100g) of OpenCV, median over 9 sizes; OpenCV wins 9/9 and 8/9.
